items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The methods used to collect and analyse information, such as surveys, interviews or document analysis"?
items.answer: methodology
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of methodology.

items.stem: Distinguish between qualitative data and quantitative data.
items.answer: Quantitative data are numerical, such as statistics; qualitative data are descriptive, such as interview responses.
items.markingKey: Quantitative data are numerical, such as statistics; qualitative data are descriptive, such as interview responses. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Using more sources always makes an investigation better." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Quality, relevance and range of sources matter more than quantity.
items.markingKey: Quality, relevance and range of sources matter more than quantity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Methodology guide (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a university research methods guide for social science students, 2022

The guide advised that a pilot study – a small trial of a questionnaire or interview – helps researchers find confusing questions, estimate how long data collection will take and improve the reliability of their methods.

What is the message of Source A about formulating a research question and planning an investigation (Criterion B)? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: Piloting improves the quality and reliability of research.
items.markingKey: Piloting improves the quality and reliability of research. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Mohammed argues that "Primary research is more valuable than secondary research in an MYP investigation." Chloé disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Both are valuable; the strongest investigations combine primary data with high-quality secondary sources.
items.markingKey: Mohammed: it produces original, specific data. Chloé: samples are often small and unrepresentative. Judgement (1-2 marks): Both are valuable; the strongest investigations combine primary data with high-quality secondary sources.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What happened at Fukushima?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into formulating a research question and planning an investigation (Criterion B). Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a descriptive question Improved: "How did the 2011 Fukushima disaster affect Germany's energy policy?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a descriptive question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How did the 2011 Fukushima disaster affect Germany's energy policy?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Primary research is more valuable than secondary research in an MYP investigation."
items.answer: Thesis: Both are valuable; the strongest investigations combine primary data with high-quality secondary sources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it produces original, specific data; it develops investigating skills. Counter-arguments: samples are often small and unrepresentative; secondary sources provide context and expert analysis. Thesis/conclusion: Both are valuable; the strongest investigations combine primary data with high-quality secondary sources. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "To what extent did the Delhi Metro reduce road traffic in Delhi between 2002 and 2020?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Use ridership data, traffic counts and two studies; evaluate; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use ridership data, traffic counts and two studies; evaluate; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Define the term "reflection".
items.answer: Evaluating the process and results of an investigation and how it could be improved
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: evaluating the process and results of an investigation and how it could be improved. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why researchers evaluate their process.
items.answer: Reflecting on what worked and what did not helps assess how reliable the findings are and how future investigations could be improved.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reflecting on what worked and what did not helps assess how reliable the findings are and how future investigations could be improved. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why ethical considerations matter in research.
items.answer: Participants must be protected from harm, their privacy respected and their consent obtained; academic honesty requires acknowledging sources.
items.markingKey: Content: Participants must be protected from harm, their privacy respected and their consent obtained; academic honesty requires acknowledging sources. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "historiography"?
options: Combining knowledge and methods from different subjects, such as history, geography and economics
An opposing view that the writer acknowledges and responds to
The on-screen examination for MYP year 5, with tasks testing all four criteria
The study of how historians' interpretations of the past differ and change
items.answer: The study of how historians' interpretations of the past differ and change
items.markingKey: D. "historiography" is the study of how historians' interpretations of the past differ and change.

items.stem: Distinguish between the value of a source and its limitation.
items.answer: Value is how a source helps answer a question; limitation is what reduces its usefulness for that question.
items.markingKey: Value is how a source helps answer a question; limitation is what reduces its usefulness for that question. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why historians' interpretations change over time.
items.answer: New sources become available, such as Soviet archives after 1991, new methods and questions emerge, and historians are influenced by their own context.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: New sources become available, such as Soviet archives after 1991, new methods and questions emerge, and historians are influenced by their own context. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Primary sources are always more reliable than secondary sources." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Primary sources may be biased or limited; secondary sources may be more balanced, drawing on many primary sources.
items.markingKey: Primary sources may be biased or limited; secondary sources may be more balanced, drawing on many primary sources. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Photograph (described): Photograph taken by a press photographer for an international news agency, Berlin, 10 November 1989

A black-and-white photograph shows a crowd of young people standing on the Berlin Wall at the Brandenburg Gate at night, some holding champagne bottles and others chipping at the concrete with hammers.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into evaluating sources: origin, purpose, value and limitation (OPVL), referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Photograph taken by a press photographer for an international news agency, Berlin, 10 November 1989. Purpose: to record and report a major news event for newspapers worldwide. Value: It provides visual evidence of the public mood immediately after the Wall opened. Limitation: It captures one moment and place selected by the photographer; it does not show the views of East German leaders or people elsewhere.
items.markingKey: Origin: Photograph taken by a press photographer for an international news agency, Berlin, 10 November 1989. Purpose: to record and report a major news event for newspapers worldwide. Value: It provides visual evidence of the public mood immediately after the Wall opened. Limitation: It captures one moment and place selected by the photographer; it does not show the views of East German leaders or people elsewhere. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why a source can be valuable even if it is unreliable.
items.answer: An unreliable source can still reveal attitudes, beliefs or propaganda techniques, which may be what the investigation is about.
items.markingKey: Content: An unreliable source can still reveal attitudes, beliefs or propaganda techniques, which may be what the investigation is about. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Primary sources are always more useful than secondary sources for historical inquiry."
items.answer: Usefulness depends on the question; strong inquiry uses both, evaluating each critically.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they provide direct evidence from the time; they reveal contemporary attitudes. Arguments against: secondary sources offer context, synthesis and expert analysis; primary sources can be partial, biased or forged. Supported judgement: Usefulness depends on the question; strong inquiry uses both, evaluating each critically.

items.stem: Explain why the purpose of a source affects its value.
items.answer: A source created to persuade, such as propaganda or a campaign speech, may select or distort information, but it is valuable for understanding the creator's aims and audience.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A source created to persuade, such as propaganda or a campaign speech, may select or distort information, but it is valuable for understanding the creator's aims and audience. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A biased source should never be used." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All sources have perspectives; biased sources are valuable for studying attitudes and must be used critically.
items.markingKey: All sources have perspectives; biased sources are valuable for studying attitudes and must be used critically. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How have historians' interpretations of the origins of the Cold War changed since the opening of Soviet archives in the 1990s?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Read orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist historians; compare arguments and evidence; evaluate; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist historians; compare arguments and evidence; evaluate; cite in MLA. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Where should the main argument normally be stated in an essay?
items.answer: In the introduction, as a thesis
items.markingKey: In the introduction, as a thesis. It is then developed throughout.

items.stem: Suggest and justify the most appropriate graph or map to present data on whether countries with higher GDP per capita have higher life expectancy. State two features your graph must include.
items.answer: A scatter graph – it shows the relationship (correlation) between two variables
items.markingKey: A scatter graph (1); justification: it shows the relationship (correlation) between two variables (1); features (1): title, labelled axes with units or key, scale, source of data. Criterion C ii.

items.stem: "The conclusion should introduce new evidence." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The conclusion should weigh the arguments already made and answer the question.
items.markingKey: The conclusion should weigh the arguments already made and answer the question. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student chose the research question "To what extent was the Marshall Plan motivated by US economic self-interest rather than humanitarian concern?" Explain two reasons why this question is relevant and worth investigating.
items.answer: It requires weighing motives and perspectives in an extended argument.
items.markingKey: It requires weighing motives and perspectives in an extended argument. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "To what extent was the Marshall Plan motivated by US economic self-interest rather than humanitarian concern?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Use speeches, US congressional debates, trade data and two historians; plan argument and counter-argument; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use speeches, US congressional debates, trade data and two historians; plan argument and counter-argument; cite in MLA. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A clear thesis is the most important feature of an extended response."
items.answer: A clear thesis is essential, but it must be supported by evidence, analysis and engagement with other views to produce a strong response.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives the essay direction and focus; it shows the writer is answering the question. Arguments against: evidence and analysis are needed to support it; counter-arguments and a judgement show critical thinking. items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "A clear thesis is the most important feature of an extended response."
items.answer: Thesis: A clear thesis is essential, but it must be supported by evidence, analysis and engagement with other views to produce a strong response.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives the essay direction and focus; it shows the writer is answering the question. items.stem: Briefly explain why a strong essay includes counter-arguments.
items.answer: Acknowledging and responding to opposing views shows understanding of complexity and strengthens the writer's judgement.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Acknowledging and responding to opposing views shows understanding of complexity and strengthens the writer's judgement. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student wants to present data on the number of international tourists visiting six different countries in 2019. Which is the most appropriate way to present it?
options: A climate graph (bars for rainfall, line for temperature)
items.answer: A bar chart
items.markingKey: C. A bar chart: it compares separate categories.

items.stem: Which command term asks you to break down information to bring out its structure and relationships?
items.answer: Analyse
items.markingKey: Analyse. Analyse is a Criterion D term.

items.stem: A student claims: "All questions should get equal time." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Time should be allocated according to marks.
items.markingKey: Time should be allocated according to marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why planning is important even under time pressure.
items.answer: A short plan ensures a clear argument, relevant evidence and balance, and prevents running out of time on extended responses. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A short plan ensures a clear argument, relevant evidence and balance, and prevents running out of time on extended responses. items.stem: A student chose the research question "How far do differences in public health spending explain differences in life expectancy between Kerala and Uttar Pradesh?" Explain two reasons why this question is relevant and worth investigating.
items.answer: It investigates a development issue using comparable data.
items.markingKey: It investigates a development issue using comparable data. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How far do differences in public health spending explain differences in life expectancy between Kerala and Uttar Pradesh?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use NFHS and state budget data and two studies; compare indicators; evaluate data; cite in APA.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "On-screen examinations are a fair way to assess MYP Individuals and Societies." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: eAssessment offers a standardised measure of key skills, but it complements rather than replaces the sustained inquiry assessed in coursework.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they test all criteria with varied, real-world stimulus; they are standardised and externally moderated. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which command term asks you to give a brief account or summary?

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ethical research"?

Combining knowledge and methods from different subjects, such as history, geography and economics
Evaluating the process and results of an investigation and how it could be improved
Words and phrases that guide the reader through an argument, such as "however", "furthermore" and "therefore"

items.markingKey: Content: A short plan ensures a clear argument, relevant evidence and balance, and prevents running out of time on extended responses. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Primary research is more valuable than secondary research in an MYP investigation."
items.answer: Both are valuable; the strongest investigations combine primary data with high-quality secondary sources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it produces original, specific data; it develops investigating skills. Arguments against: samples are often small and unrepresentative; secondary sources provide context and expert analysis. Supported judgement: Both are valuable; the strongest investigations combine primary data with high-quality secondary sources.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Primary sources are always more useful than secondary sources for historical inquiry."
items.answer: Thesis: Usefulness depends on the question; strong inquiry uses both, evaluating each critically.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they provide direct evidence from the time; they reveal contemporary attitudes. Counter-arguments: secondary sources offer context, synthesis and expert analysis; primary sources can be partial, biased or forged. Thesis/conclusion: Usefulness depends on the question; strong inquiry uses both, evaluating each critically. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Assessment guidance (paraphrased): Paraphrase of typical IB MYP Individuals and Societies eAssessment markband descriptors for extended response tasks

The guidance stated that the highest-scoring responses present a sustained, well-supported argument that consistently addresses the question, use relevant and accurate evidence, consider different perspectives and reach a well-reasoned conclusion.

"A clear thesis is the most important feature of an extended response." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: A clear thesis is essential, but it must be supported by evidence, analysis and engagement with other views to produce a strong response.
items.markingKey: From the source: Strong responses are sustained, supported, balanced and reach a reasoned conclusion. Own knowledge for: it gives the essay direction and focus; it shows the writer is answering the question. Own knowledge against: evidence and analysis are needed to support it; counter-arguments and a judgement show critical thinking. Judgement: A clear thesis is essential, but it must be supported by evidence, analysis and engagement with other views to produce a strong response. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "On-screen examinations are a fair way to assess MYP Individuals and Societies." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: eAssessment offers a standardised measure of key skills, but it complements rather than replaces the sustained inquiry assessed in coursework.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they test all criteria with varied, real-world stimulus; they are standardised and externally moderated. Arguments against: they test skills under time pressure rather than sustained inquiry; students' typing skills and access to technology vary. Supported judgement: eAssessment offers a standardised measure of key skills, but it complements rather than replaces the sustained inquiry assessed in coursework. Markbands (12 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which command term asks students to give valid reasons or evidence for an answer?
items.answer: Justify
items.markingKey: C. Justify the relevance of a research question.

items.stem: A Soviet propaganda poster is most valuable for which question?
options: How the Soviet government wanted to present itself
items.answer: How the Soviet government wanted to present itself
items.markingKey: C. Purpose determines value.

items.stem: What is the best way to include a counter-argument?
options: Mention it only in the bibliography
Agree with every view equally without a judgement
Present it fairly, then explain why it is weaker or how it modifies your argument
items.answer: Present it fairly, then explain why it is weaker or how it modifies your argument
items.markingKey: D. This shows critical thinking.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the eAssessment combines history, geography and economics.
items.answer: MYP Individuals and Societies is an integrated subject, so tasks test the ability to apply concepts across disciplines to real-world issues.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: MYP Individuals and Societies is an integrated subject, so tasks test the ability to apply concepts across disciplines to real-world issues. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Using more sources always makes an investigation better." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Quality, relevance and range of sources matter more than quantity.
items.markingKey: Quality, relevance and range of sources matter more than quantity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between its limitation and the value of a source.
items.answer: Value is how a source helps answer a question; limitation is what reduces its usefulness for that question.
items.markingKey: Value is how a source helps answer a question; limitation is what reduces its usefulness for that question. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between description and analysis.
items.answer: Description states what happened; analysis explains why or how and examines significance and relationships.
items.markingKey: Description states what happened; analysis explains why or how and examines significance and relationships. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between "explain" and "evaluate".
items.answer: "Explain" requires reasons or causes; "evaluate" requires weighing strengths and limitations to reach a judgement.
items.markingKey: "Explain" requires reasons or causes; "evaluate" requires weighing strengths and limitations to reach a judgement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between quantitative data and qualitative data.
items.answer: Quantitative data are numerical, such as statistics; qualitative data are descriptive, such as interview responses.
items.markingKey: Quantitative data are numerical, such as statistics; qualitative data are descriptive, such as interview responses. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of these is the correct APA (7th edition) reference for Yuval Noah Harari's book "Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind" (Harvill Secker, 2014)?
options: Yuval Noah Harari. Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind. Harvill Secker, 2014.
Harari, Y. N. (2014). Sapiens: A brief history of humankind. Harvill Secker.
Sapiens: A brief history of humankind. (2014). Harari, Y. N. Harvill Secker.
Harari, Yuval Noah. Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind. Harvill Secker, 2014.
items.answer: Harari, Y. N. (2014). Sapiens: A brief history of humankind. Harvill Secker.
items.markingKey: B. APA: Author surname, initials (year). Title in sentence case. Publisher.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into formulating a research question and planning an investigation (Criterion B)?
options: How did the 2011 Fukushima disaster affect Germany's energy policy?
items.answer: How did the 2011 Fukushima disaster affect Germany's energy policy?
items.markingKey: D. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: You used a book by William Dalrymple called "The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company", published by Bloomsbury in 2019. Write the entry for your bibliography in MLA (9th edition) format (write the title in plain text; it would be italicised in a typed document).
items.answer: Dalrymple, William. The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company. Bloomsbury, 2019.
items.markingKey: Dalrymple, William. The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company. Bloomsbury, 2019. 1 mark for correct order of elements (author, title, publisher, date at the end); 1 mark for punctuation and full first name and title case. Criterion C iii: documenting sources.

items.stem: Elena argues that "A clear thesis is the most important feature of an extended response." Leila disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.

items.markingKey: Elena: it gives the essay direction and focus. Leila: evidence and analysis are needed to support it. Judgement (1-2 marks): A clear thesis is essential, but it must be supported by evidence, analysis and engagement with other views to produce a strong response.

items.stem:
Source A – Methodology guide (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a university research methods guide for social science students, 2022

The guide advised that a pilot study – a small trial of a questionnaire or interview – helps researchers find confusing questions, estimate how long data collection will take and improve the reliability of their methods.

With reference to its origin and purpose, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a student investigating formulating a research question and planning an investigation (Criterion B).
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of a university research methods guide for social science students, 2022. Purpose: to help students plan effective primary research. Value: It gives practical, evidence-based advice. Limitation: It is general advice not tailored to MYP investigations.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of a university research methods guide for social science students, 2022. Purpose: to help students plan effective primary research. Value: It gives practical, evidence-based advice. Limitation: It is general advice not tailored to MYP investigations. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on evaluating sources: origin, purpose, value and limitation (OPVL) produced the question "Who started the Cold War?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed question Improved: "How have historians' interpretations of the origins of the Cold War changed since the opening of Soviet archives in the 1990s?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How have historians' interpretations of the origins of the Cold War changed since the opening of Soviet archives in the 1990s?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

Source A – Data source (described): Table compiled from United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report 2023/24

A table compares four countries' GDP per capita, life expectancy, mean years of schooling and HDI for 2022, using UNDP data. It shows that two countries with similar GDP per capita have different HDI values.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching eAssessment practice: source engagement, investigation and extended-response tasks? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Table compiled from United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report 2023/24. Purpose: to present comparable development indicators for analysis. Value: It uses an authoritative, standardised international data set. Limitation: Indicators are national averages that hide inequality, and data for some countries are estimates.
